title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: Two days later, on the fifteenth of July, an enormous number of carriages stood outside the Sloboda Palace.

The great halls were full. In the first were the nobility and gentry in their uniforms; in the second, bearded merchants in full-skirted blue cloth coats wearing medals. In the nobles' hall there was constant movement and a buzz of voices. The chief dignitaries sat on high-backed chairs at a large table under the portrait of the Emperor, but most of the gentry were strolling about the room.

All these nobles, whom Pierre saw every day at the Club or in their own homes, were in uniform—some in the style of Catherine's era, others in that of Emperor Paul's time, others again in the new uniforms of Alexander's reign or the ordinary uniform of the nobility—and the general effect of everyone being in uniform gave something strange and theatrical to these diverse and familiar faces, both old and young. The old men, with dim eyes, toothless mouths, bald and bloated or gaunt and wrinkled, were especially striking. For the most part they sat quietly in their places, silent, or if they walked about and talked, attached themselves to someone younger. On all these faces, as on the faces of the crowd Petya had seen in the Square, there was a striking contradiction: the general expectation of a solemn event alongside everyday concerns about a card game, Peter the cook, Zinaida Dmitrievna's health, and so on.

Pierre was there too, buttoned up since early morning in a nobleman's uniform that had become too tight. He was agitated; this extraordinary gathering not only of nobles but also of the merchant class—an assembly that reminded him of the States-General—stirred up a whole series of ideas he had long set aside but which were deeply engraved in his soul: thoughts of the Social Contract and the French Revolution. The words in the Emperor's appeal—that the sovereign was coming to the capital to consult with his people—reinforced this idea. And imagining that something important he had long been waiting for was drawing near, he strolled about watching and listening, but nowhere finding any confirmation of the ideas that occupied him.

The Emperor's manifesto was read, arousing enthusiasm, and then everyone moved about discussing it. Besides the usual topics of conversation, Pierre heard questions about where the marshals of the nobility should stand when the Emperor entered, when a ball should be given in the Emperor's honor, whether they should group themselves by district or by province... and so on; but as soon as the war was touched on, or the reason the nobility had been summoned, the talk became vague and uncertain. Then everyone preferred listening to speaking.

A middle-aged man, handsome and vigorous, in the uniform of a retired naval officer, was speaking in one of the rooms, and a small crowd had gathered around him. Pierre went up to the circle that had formed around the speaker and listened. Count Ilya Rostov, in a military uniform of Catherine's time, was strolling with his pleasant smile among the crowd, all of whom he knew. He too approached the group and listened with his usual kindly smile and nods of approval. The retired naval officer was speaking very boldly, as was evident from the listeners' expressions and from the fact that some of the meekest and quietest men Pierre knew walked away disapprovingly or expressed disagreement. Pierre pushed his way to the middle of the group, listened, and became convinced that the man was indeed a liberal, but of views quite different from his own. The naval officer spoke in a particularly rich, musical, aristocratic baritone, pleasantly swallowing his r's and slurring his consonants—the voice of a man used to calling out to his servant, "Hey! Bring me my pipe!" It suggested a life of ease and the exercise of authority.

"So what if the Smolensk people have offered to raise militia for the Emperor? Are we supposed to take Smolensk as our model? If the noble aristocracy of the province of Moscow sees fit, it can show its loyalty to the Emperor in other ways. Have we forgotten the raising of the militia in oh-seven? All it did was line the pockets of priests' sons and thieves and robbers..."
Count Ilya Rostov smiled pleasantly and nodded approval.

"And was our militia of any use to the Empire? Not at all! It only ruined our farming! Better have another draft... or our men will come back neither soldiers nor peasants, and all we'll get is moral corruption. The nobility don't begrudge their lives—every one of us will go and bring in more recruits, and the sovereign"—that was how he referred to the Emperor—"need only say the word and we'll all die for him!" added the orator with passion.

Count Rostov's mouth watered with pleasure and he nudged Pierre, but Pierre wanted to speak himself. He pushed forward, feeling stirred but not yet sure what stirred him or what he would say. He had barely opened his mouth when one of the senators—a man without a tooth in his head, with a shrewd though angry expression—standing near the first speaker, interrupted him. Clearly accustomed to managing debates and keeping arguments on track, he began in a low but distinct voice:

"I believe, sir," said the senator, mumbling with his toothless mouth, "that we have been summoned here not to debate whether it's better for the empire to adopt conscription or to call out the militia. We have been summoned to reply to the appeal with which our sovereign the Emperor has honored us. But to judge what is best—conscription or the militia—we can leave to the highest authority..."

Pierre suddenly found an outlet for his excitement. He steeled himself against the senator, who was introducing such a narrow, procedural attitude into the nobles' deliberations. Pierre stepped forward and interrupted him. He didn't yet know what he would say, but he began speaking eagerly, occasionally lapsing into French or expressing himself in bookish Russian.

"Excuse me, your excellency," he began. (He knew the senator well but thought it necessary to address him formally on this occasion.) "Though I don't agree with the gentleman"—he hesitated, wanting to say "my very honorable opponent"—"with the gentleman whom I have not the honor of knowing, I believe the nobility have been summoned not merely to express sympathy and enthusiasm but also to consider the means by which we can help our Fatherland! I believe," he went on, warming to his subject, "that the Emperor himself would not be satisfied to find in us merely owners of serfs whom we are willing to hand over for his service, and cannon fodder we are ready to make of ourselves—and not to obtain from us any co-co-counsel."
* "Cannon fodder."

Many people drew back from the circle, noticing the senator's sarcastic smile and the boldness of Pierre's remarks. Only Count Rostov was pleased—as he had been pleased with the naval officer, the senator, and in general with whatever speech he had most recently heard.

"I think that before discussing these questions," Pierre continued, "we should ask the Emperor—most respectfully ask His Majesty—to let us know the number of our troops and the position our army and our forces are now in, and then..."

But Pierre had barely uttered these words before he was attacked from three sides. The most vigorous attack came from an old acquaintance—a card player who had always been friendly to him—Stepan Stepanovich Adraksin. Adraksin was in uniform, and whether because of it or some other cause, Pierre saw a completely different man before him. With a sudden expression of malice on his aged face, Adraksin shouted at Pierre:

"In the first place, I tell you we have no right to question the Emperor about that, and secondly, even if the Russian nobility had that right, the Emperor could not answer such a question. The troops are moved according to the enemy's movements, and their numbers increase and decrease..."

Another voice—that of a nobleman of medium height, about forty years old, whom Pierre had formerly met at the gypsies' and knew as a bad card player—also transformed by his uniform—came up and interrupted Adraksin.

"Yes, and this is no time for discussion," he continued, "but for action: there is war in Russia! The enemy is advancing to destroy Russia, to desecrate the graves of our fathers, to carry off our wives and children." The nobleman beat his chest. "We will all rise—every one of us will go—for our father the Tsar!" he shouted, rolling his bloodshot eyes. Several approving voices were heard in the crowd. "We are Russians and will not begrudge our blood in defense of our faith, the throne, and the Fatherland! We must stop raving if we are sons of our Fatherland! We will show Europe how Russia rises to defend Russia!"
Pierre wished to reply but couldn't get a word in. He felt that his words, regardless of their meaning, were less audible than his opponent's voice.
Count Rostov, at the back of the crowd, was expressing approval; several people, briskly turning away from the speaker at the end of each phrase, said:
"That's right, quite right! Exactly!"

Pierre wanted to say that he was ready to sacrifice his money, his serfs, even himself—only one needed to understand the situation in order to improve it—but he couldn't speak. Many voices shouted and talked at the same time, so that Count Rostov didn't have time to approve them all, and the group grew, broke apart, reformed, and then moved with a hum of talk into the largest hall and toward the great table. Not only was Pierre's attempt to speak unsuccessful, but he was rudely interrupted, pushed aside, and people turned away from him as from a common enemy. This wasn't because they were displeased by what he had said—his speech had already been forgotten after the many that followed—but the crowd needed a visible object to love and a visible object to hate. Pierre became the latter. Many other orators spoke after the excited nobleman, all in the same tone. Many spoke eloquently and originally.

Glinka, the editor of the Russian Messenger, who was recognized (cries of "Author! Author!" were heard in the crowd), said that "hell must be repelled by hell" and that he had seen a child smile at lightning flashes and thunderclaps, but "we will not be that child."
"Yes, yes, at thunderclaps!" was repeated approvingly in the back rows.

The crowd moved up to the great table, at which sat gray-haired or bald seventy-year-old dignitaries in uniforms and sashes, nearly all of whom Pierre had seen in their homes with their jesters or playing cards at the Club. With a constant hum of voices the crowd pressed toward the table. Squeezed by the throng against the high-backed chairs, the orators spoke one after another, and sometimes two at once. Those standing behind noticed what a speaker failed to say and rushed to supply it. Others in that heat and crush racked their brains for some thought and hurried to voice it. The old dignitaries, whom Pierre knew, sat and turned to look first at one speaker and then at another, and their faces mostly showed nothing except that they found it very hot. Pierre, however, felt excited, and the general desire to show readiness for any sacrifice—which found expression more in tone and looks than in the substance of the speeches—infected him too. He did not give up his opinions, but felt himself somehow at fault and wanted to justify himself.
"I only said that it would make more sense to make sacrifices when we know what is actually needed!" he said, trying to be heard above the other voices.
One of the old men nearest him glanced around, but his attention was immediately drawn away by an exclamation from the other side of the table.
"Yes, Moscow will be surrendered! She will be our atonement!" shouted one man.
"He is the enemy of mankind!" cried another. "Let me speak..." "Gentlemen, you're crushing me!..."
